title: Prebuilt DuckDB artifact: split load_all_data into a build step and a load step
description:
The largest Lambda liability, and a win on the current self-hosted deployment regardless of target.

Today load_all_data() (data_model.py:301-314) reads 531MB of CSVs into an in-memory DuckDB on every process start: loads 19 years of expenditures, canonicalizes 76,930 payee variants to 76,818 canonical names, applies data-quality flags, loads 6 enrichment tables, and builds 8 summary tables. Measured on this repo: 8.7s cold init (1.9s import + 5.9s load + 0.3s schema), 1.94GB peak RSS, 2,257,399 expenditure rows.

Lambda soft-limits the INIT phase at ~10s before re-running init inside (and billing) the invocation, so this must come down.

Measured with a prebuilt file-backed DuckDB instead: 113MB artifact, 0.41s to open read-only and rebuild the prompt schema, 2.40s total cold init including imports, 415MB peak RSS, 0.031s for a top-10 payee aggregate over 2.26M rows. Offline materialize took 11.2s once.

Also directly addresses louisville-open-data-41y (cold start exceeds 4 min under host load) and the root cause of the 2026-08-11 502 outage.
design:
Add a --materialize <path> mode that runs the existing chain (_load_expenditures -> _apply_canonicalization -> _apply_data_quality -> _load_enrichment -> _build_summaries) against a file-backed connection instead of duckdb.connect(). Add load_prebuilt(path) that opens it read-only.

CRITICAL GOTCHA, found while measuring: load_all_data ends with SET enable_external_access = false (data_model.py:313) and that setting is IRREVERSIBLE on a connection - attaching a file afterwards fails with PermissionException. The lockdown must move to the load path only, never the build path.

Keep the CSV path working for local dev and for refresh_data.py. The prebuilt file becomes a build artifact produced by CI and baked into the image.
acceptance_criteria: python -m pytest -q passes against a prebuilt artifact. Cold init from the artifact under 3s and peak RSS under 600MB, measured. The CSV path still works unchanged for local dev.
notes:
DONE 2026-08-28.

Implementation (data_model.py):
  _ingest()         shared build chain, so the CSV and artifact paths cannot drift
  _lock_down()      the irreversible SET enable_external_access=false, now applied
                    ONLY on serving connections (was inline in load_all_data)
  build_database()  CSVs -> DuckDB file, atomic via <path>.building + os.replace,
                    with cleanup of the partial file on failure
  load_prebuilt()   opens read-only + locked down; FileNotFoundError names the
                    --materialize command
  __main__          python data_model.py --materialize PATH [--data-dir DIR],
                    which verifies the artifact opens and is non-empty before
                    reporting success

app.py: PREBUILT_DB env var. Set -> load_prebuilt; unset -> load_all_data.
Deliberately NO fallback when the file is missing: on a container sized for the
artifact the CSV rebuild is what exhausts memory and overruns the health-check
start period (the 2026-08-11 outage). Fail loud at boot instead.

MEASURED (this repo, real data):
  artifact             112 MB   (from 531 MB of CSVs)
  offline build        8.3s
  app boot on artifact 0.29s    (vs ~8s on the CSV path)
  load_prebuilt open   0.01s
  cold init (import+open+schema+year_context) 0.60-2.40s depending on page cache
  peak RSS             403 MB   (vs 1.94 GB)
  full scan aggregate  0.03s over 2.26M rows
  ACCEPTANCE: cold init <3s PASS, peak RSS <600MB PASS

EQUIVALENCE proven, not assumed: compact schema description and year_context are
byte-identical between the two paths, and 8 query result sets (raw table,
canonical columns, data-quality flags, every summary table) hash-match.

The two _-prefixed canonicalization helpers are CREATE TEMP TABLE in city.yaml,
so the artifact has 15 tables vs 17 in-memory. Correct, not a loss: they are
build-time intermediates already excluded from the prompt schema.

Tests: tests/test_prebuilt_db.py, 19 new (suite 504 -> 523, all passing).
Covers read-only enforcement, filesystem-escape blocking (read_csv/read_json/
COPY TO all rejected - read_only=True alone does NOT block these), atomic build,
stale-temp recovery, and CSV-vs-artifact equivalence.

The atomicity test caught a real defect during development: a failed build left
its .building file behind. Fixed.

Docs: CLAUDE.md 'Prebuilt database artifact' section, .env.example.
NOT YET DONE: nothing wires this into a container or CI - that is n8w.
close_reason: Implemented, measured, and tested. Cold init 8.7s/1.94GB -> 0.29s app boot/403MB. Equivalence to the CSV path proven byte-identical.

title: Spike: verify SSE survives Lambda Web Adapter + Function URL + CloudFront
description:
GATES THE ENTIRE MIGRATION. Run before any other build work.

The product is token-by-token streaming: /api/ask returns a StreamingResponse over a sync generator (app.py:1029, app.py:1453) and the frontend reads it incrementally via fetch + ReadableStream.getReader() (static/index.html:1270,1300). Mangum, the usual FastAPI-on-Lambda shim, BUFFERS - it would hold the whole ~40s answer and emit it at once, destroying the core UX.

The intended path is AWS Lambda Web Adapter with AWS_LWA_INVOKE_MODE=response_stream plus InvokeMode RESPONSE_STREAM on the Function URL, which requires a container image. Native managed-runtime response streaming (awslambda.streamifyResponse) is Node.js only, so LWA is the only Python route.

The specific unverified risk is CloudFront: it sits in front of the Function URL and its buffering behaviour for chunked/streamed origin responses must be confirmed empirically, not assumed.
design:
Minimal spike, throwaway code - do NOT build the real app here. A hello-world FastAPI that yields an SSE event once per second for 30s, packaged as a container image with LWA, deployed behind a Function URL, then behind CloudFront with OAC.

Measure time-to-first-byte and inter-chunk arrival at each hop: (1) direct Function URL, (2) through CloudFront. If chunks arrive batched at either hop, try CloudFront policy adjustments; if still batched, the target flips to Cloud Run and this epic is re-planned.
acceptance_criteria: curl against the CloudFront URL shows SSE events arriving incrementally over ~30s, not in one batch at the end. Time-to-first-byte under 2s. Result documented on this issue either way, including the negative case.

title: 502 outage: autoheal kill-loop on louisville-bot + add service-level dead-man's-switch alert
description: Prod went down with Cloudflare 502 (2026-08-11 ~15:01 UTC). Root cause: container health check start-period 120s < slow startup (~5min under host pressure); autoheal restart-looped it, final restart failed leaving container Exited(255); restart policy did not revive it. Machine-level healthchecks.io heartbeat did not fire because the Air itself was up. Fix: (1) restart container (done), (2) recreate with --health-start-period 600s, (3) add louisville-bot service heartbeat: launchd agent pings healthchecks.io only if https://louisville.raylytics.io/api/health responds, with ntfy max-priority + email on silence.
close_reason: Site restored and alerting shipped. Root cause: health-start-period 120s was shorter than the >4min cold start under host load, so autoheal restart-looped the container from 10:23-11:00 UTC and its final restart failed, leaving it Exited(255) where --restart unless-stopped did not revive it. Fixed: container recreated with --health-start-period 600s; new healthchecks.io service check + LaunchAgent heartbeat that probes the public URL; self-heal for the exited-container case. Alert chain verified end-to-end (max-priority ntfy DOWN + email, auto UP on recovery).

title: Refine pass: prefer Cerebras (paid) over free OpenRouter
description: The refine pass dominated a slow production answer (78.3s of ~107s) because OpenRouter's free nemotron dribbles tokens. description: When a query returns 0 rows or a single row whose aggregates are all NULL, extract the string literals in the SQL, check each against the value index, and re-generate once with a hint listing what matched nothing and the closest real values. title: Value grounding: index categorical vocabularies and inject question-matched values into SQL generation
description: spend_category (979 values), expenditure_category, fund (246), jobTitle etc. are never shown to the model (compact schema enumerates only <=12-value columns), so it guesses literals like ILIKE '%Vehicle%' that match nothing. Build a _value_index table at load time (table, column, value, weight, rows) for categorical VARCHAR columns; per question, extract terms (+ pack-defined synonyms) and inject the matching real values into the SQL-generation user message. No extra LLM call.

title: [epic] Portfolio-grade accuracy & reliability pass (2026-08-30)
description: Review of the agentic analytics experience on 2026-08-30 found a confident wrong answer in production: 'How much did Louisville Fire spend on vehicles in FY2024?' produced spend_category ILIKE '%Vehicle%' (0 matches, SUM=NULL) and the bot answered 'no recorded vehicle spending' when the true figure is ~$1.58M across Automotive Parts/Fuel/Repair categories. Root causes: (1) the prompt never shows high-cardinality categorical vocabularies (spend_category has 979 values), so the model guesses literals; (2) there is no verify-and-repair step when a filter matches nothing — the prompt tells the model to re-query but the pipeline runs exactly one SQL; (3) an all-NULL single-row aggregate is not treated as an empty result. Also: no README.md in a public repo, no LLM-in-the-loop eval harness, untrimmed spend_category values. This epic tracks the fixes.

title: Rotate LLM and admin secrets into SSM Parameter Store during the AWS migration
description:
## Why this needs you (please confirm this is accurate)

The three runtime secrets — `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, `CEREBRAS_PAID_API_KEY`,
`ADMIN_TOKEN` — need to be rotated at the provider and written into SSM
Parameter Store as SecureStrings. I cannot log into OpenRouter or Cerebras to
issue new keys, and I should not handle the values at all.

Rotation (rather than copy-across) is the right call because the current values
have lived in a gitignored `.env` and, more importantly, on a `docker run`
command line — which means they have been visible in shell history and in
`docker inspect` output on the Air. A migration is the natural moment to cycle
them.

No code change is needed on my side: all three are already read via
`os.environ` (`analytics_agent.py:1049-1126`, `app.py:768`), so this is
pure wiring.

## Steps

1. Issue a **new** OpenRouter key; do not reuse the current one.
   Confirm its tier with:
   `curl -s https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/key -H "Authorization: Bearer $NEW_KEY"`
   (`is_free_tier` tells you which cap applies — 50/day free, 1000/day after
   $10 of credits).

2. Issue a new Cerebras key. Note the prepaid balance figure somewhere you will
   see it — the key stops at zero with HTTP 402 and no auto-recharge, so
   depletion is a silent outage. That alerting is tracked separately as
   louisville-open-data-8uk.

3. Generate a fresh `ADMIN_TOKEN` (any long random secret, e.g.
   `openssl rand -hex 32`). It gates `/api/cache`, and `warm_cache.py` and
   `refresh_data.py` must run with the same value in their env.

4. Write all three to SSM Parameter Store as **SecureString**, under a
   consistent prefix, e.g. `/lou/prod/OPENROUTER_API_KEY`.

5. Revoke the old OpenRouter and Cerebras keys once the new stack answers a
   real question.

6. **Do not paste any of these values into this issue, into chat, or into a
   commit.** Tell me the parameter *paths* only; I will wire the Lambda
   execution role to read them.

7. Close this issue when complete.

## What unblocks me when this returns

Three SSM parameter paths. With those I can finish the IaC in
louisville-open-data-i0q (execution-role read permissions plus env wiring) and
run the cutover verification in louisville-open-data-lla.

title: Provision the AWS account and IaC bootstrap for the Lou migration
description:
## Why this needs you (please confirm this is accurate)

The migration needs an IAM identity I cannot create. Creating users, roles, and
access keys is a human action by design — and `iam:CreateAccessKey` is on the
agent's hard-deny list, so this cannot be delegated even accidentally.

**Decided 2026-08-28:** deploy into existing account **012146975534**
(`us-east-1`), as a dedicated `lou-deploy` role — *not* as the `airflow-user`
key the workstation's `default` profile uses.

Full least-privilege setup, with runnable commands and the policy JSON, is in
**`infra/iam/README.md`** (committed). Summary of what it creates:

- user `lou-dev` — can do nothing but assume `lou-deploy`, MFA required
- role `lou-deploy` — carries `LouServicePolicy`, the deploy-time ceiling
- policy `LouServicePolicy` — scoped to `lou-*` / `Lou*` / `/lou/` names
- policy `LouPermissionsBoundary` — the runtime ceiling, forced onto every role
  the stack creates, which is what makes granting `iam:CreateRole` safe

## Steps

1. Follow `infra/iam/README.md` steps 0–6 **as an account administrator**, not
   as `lou-dev`. `lou-deploy` deliberately cannot bootstrap CDK (bootstrap
   creates roles outside the `/lou/` path) — that is intentional, not a gap.

2. Note step 6: the default `cdk bootstrap` grants its execution role
   **AdministratorAccess**, which would silently undo the whole exercise. The
   documented command overrides it with `--cloudformation-execution-policies`
   and uses the `lou0` qualifier so Lou gets its own bootstrap roles.

3. Run the step 7 negative tests. Three commands that must be DENIED and one
   that must succeed. If a denial does not happen, tell me — the scoping is
   wrong and I would rather fix it before anything is built on it.

4. **Billing alarm**: set it on a `Project=lou` cost-allocation filter, not the
   account total — Airflow's spend would otherwise mask Lou's entirely. And
   activate the `Project` tag in Billing → Cost Allocation Tags **before the
   first deploy**: activation is not retroactive, so untagged early spend can
   never be attributed.

5. Record here: the profile name (expected `lou`) and confirmation that step 7
   behaved. **No key material in this issue or in chat** — a profile alias is
   all I need.

6. Close this issue when complete.

## What unblocks me when this returns

A working `--profile lou`. With it I can run the streaming spike
(louisville-open-data-4l4), which gates the whole migration, then build the
stack in louisville-open-data-i0q.

Already done and needing nothing from AWS: louisville-open-data-e5n (prebuilt
DuckDB artifact) is closed — app boot 8.7s/1.94GB -> 0.29s/403MB.

## Prior description (preserved on handoff)

## Why this needs you (please confirm this is accurate)

Everything in the AWS Lambda migration epic (louisville-open-data-ru6) needs an
AWS account that exists, has billing configured, and has an IAM principal the
IaC can deploy as. I cannot create an AWS account, accept its terms, attach a
payment method, or bootstrap root-level IAM — those need your identity and your

which gates the whole migration, cannot run without somewhere to deploy.

Push back if you would rather use an existing account than a fresh one — that
changes the isolation story but not the work.

## Steps

1. Create (or nominate) the AWS account this will live in. A dedicated account
   is cleaner for cost attribution and for the portfolio story, but an existing

2. Set a **billing alarm** before anything else is deployed. The analysis

3. Confirm the region. `us-east-1` is the default recommendation: CloudFront
   certificates must live there, and it has the widest service availability.

4. Create an IAM principal for IaC deploys — ideally an IAM Identity Center

   If CDK is chosen, run `cdk bootstrap` once against the account/region.

5. Record here: account ID, region, and how the deploy principal is accessed

6. Close this issue when complete.

## What unblocks me when this returns

An account ID, a region, and a named local AWS profile (or SSO config) that has

BLOCKER HIT AND FIXED 2026-08-30 — step 2 failed with LimitExceeded.

aws iam create-policy rejected LouServicePolicy: 'Cannot exceed quota for
PolicySize: 6144'. The combined deploy policy measured 6680 characters. IAM does
NOT count whitespace toward that limit, so minifying or reformatting cannot
help — only removing content or splitting can.

Split by concern rather than shrunk, because the README already tells you to
expect one or two missing actions on first deploy; trimming to just under 6144
would put you right back at LimitExceeded mid-deploy.

  LouDeployGuardrails   8 stmts, 2113 chars — IAM/STS grants and every Deny.
                       Deliberately small, should change rarely.

Safe because both are attached to lou-deploy together and passed together to
cdk bootstrap, IAM evaluates them as one identity policy, and an explicit Deny
in either overrides an Allow in the other.

WHAT YOU MUST DO DIFFERENTLY:
  - re-run ./infra/iam/render.sh (file names changed)
  - step 2 now creates THREE policies, not two
  - if LouServicePolicy was already created, delete it first (command in README)
  - step 3 attaches BOTH deploy policies
  - step 6 passes both, comma-separated, to --cloudformation-execution-policies

render.sh now runs infra/iam/check_size.py and fails loudly if any policy would
exceed the limit, so this surfaces before the aws call rather than as
LimitExceeded partway through setup. tests/test_iam_policies.py grew a size
assertion plus an overlap check, and its deploy-side assertions now run against
the UNION of both files so a future re-split cannot silently stop testing a
control. 33 IAM tests, 13/13 mutation-verified. Suite 546 -> 556.

title: Cutover: parallel deploy, warm cache, end-to-end verify, DNS
description:
Final step. Runs only after every other task in the epic is closed.

The repo has an existing deploy-verification discipline (CLAUDE.md, Deploy verification MANDATORY) that applies unchanged here. Loading / proves static files only; it does NOT prove the API works - the Cloudflare /api WAF block is the documented precedent for the edge serving the page fine while blocking the API path.

Sequence:
1. Deploy the Lambda stack in parallel with the running container. Do not touch DNS.
2. Run warm_cache.py against the new CloudFront URL to populate the shared DynamoDB cache before any real traffic.
3. Verify end-to-end against the NEW url, not localhost and not the LAN IP: /api/health returns ok; POST /api/ask with an empty question returns HTTP 200 and content-type text/event-stream (short-circuits with no LLM call, so it is a free probe); one real question in a browser returns a streamed answer with a chart.
4. Confirm streaming is genuinely incremental in the browser, not batched - the whole point of louisville-open-data-4l4.
5. Move louisville.raylytics.io DNS from the cloudflared tunnel to CloudFront.
6. Keep the container stopped-but-present for rollback, matching the existing docker rename louisville-bot-prev pattern.
7. Decommission only after a week of clean monitoring.
design:
Rollback plan is DNS: point the hostname back at the cloudflared tunnel and start the old container. Keep the louisville-data, louisville-state and louisville-logs volumes intact until decommission - louisville-state holds the response cache and stats that would otherwise be lost.

Cloudflare stays as DNS. Decide whether it keeps proxying in front of CloudFront or becomes DNS-only; proxying through both adds a hop and a second place for an /api block to hide.
acceptance_criteria: A real question answered through louisville.raylytics.io with visibly incremental streaming. Both monitors green for 24h. Rollback tested at least once before DNS moves.

title: Re-point monitoring at the new URL and add CloudWatch alarms
description:
The existing monitoring exists because the 2026-08-11 502 outage ran 5 hours unnoticed. It must not lapse during the migration.

Three pieces to re-point:
1. monitoring/louisville-bot-heartbeat.sh - a 60s LaunchAgent dead-mans switch that pings healthchecks.io only if /api/health returns ok AND POST /api/ask returns 200. It also runs docker start as a self-heal, which becomes meaningless on Lambda and should be removed. Decide whether this stays on the Air or becomes an EventBridge-triggered Lambda.
2. .github/workflows/uptime.yml - runs every 30 min, asserts on status, model_fallback and errors_last_hour.
3. The healthchecks.io check period and grace.

Note the heartbeat is 43,200 invocations/month and is over half the projected Lambda compute. It also means scale-to-zero is partly notional, since the function stays warm most of the time. Consider a 5-minute interval, or probing a static CloudFront path instead of the function.

Also carry forward louisville-open-data-8uk (alert before Cerebras credits run out) - the key is prepaid with no auto-recharge, so depletion is a silent outage, not a charge.
design:
Add CloudWatch alarms on Lambda errors, throttles, and duration p99. Alarm on WAF blocked-request spikes as the abuse signal. Keep the external healthchecks.io probe - an external dead-mans switch catches failure modes internal AWS alarms cannot, which is exactly the lesson of 2026-08-11.

Do NOT change the /api/health response shape here; louisville-open-data-far owns preserving it.
acceptance_criteria: Both probes hit the new URL and pass. A deliberately broken deploy fires an alert within 5 minutes. The docker start self-heal is removed from the heartbeat script.

title: Infrastructure as code: Lambda, Function URL, CloudFront, S3, DynamoDB
description:
Define the whole stack as code. This is also the primary portfolio artifact of the migration.

Scope: Lambda function (container image, 2048MB, reserved concurrency as a cost circuit breaker), Function URL with InvokeMode RESPONSE_STREAM, CloudFront distribution with Origin Access Control in front of it, S3 for the CSV build inputs and optionally static assets, DynamoDB tables for the cache and rate limiter, CloudWatch log group with 7-day retention, and the WAF rate rule.

Explicit non-goals, from the analysis: NO VPC and NO NAT Gateway. A VPC-attached Lambda would need a NAT (~32 dollars/month) to keep reaching OpenRouter and Cerebras, which alone breaks the ~0 dollars idle target. NO API Gateway REST - its 29s hard timeout cannot serve a request path that runs up to 230s.
design:
CDK (Python, matching the codebase) or Terraform. CDK is likely the better resume signal and keeps the language consistent.

Memory sizing: 415MB measured peak RSS on the prebuilt artifact, but Lambda vCPU scales with memory, so 2048MB is the starting point - more memory shortens every LLM-bound path and may be cheaper in GB-seconds, not more expensive. Tune empirically after the first deploy.

Set reserved concurrency deliberately (e.g. 10). At ~460 GB-s for a worst-case request it is the hard ceiling that keeps a burst from eating the free tier.
acceptance_criteria: Stack deploys from an empty account with one command. Destroy and redeploy reproduces a working service. Reserved concurrency, log retention, and the WAF rule are all in code, not console-clicked.

title: Build the Lambda container image (prebuilt DB, FTS baked, HOME=/tmp, LWA)
description:
Package the app as a Lambda container image. A container is mandatory, not a preference: measured dependencies are ~152MB unzipped (pandas 56.9, duckdb native .so 39.8, numpy 27.5, pydantic 12.5, openai 6.8, fastapi+starlette 1.5, rest ~7.4) plus the 113MB DB artifact = ~265MB, over the 250MB zip limit. The Lambda Web Adapter streaming path requires a container anyway, so this costs nothing extra. Image limit is 10GB.

Carry forward two things the existing Dockerfile already gets right:
1. The DuckDB FTS extension is baked at build time with an INSTALL AND a LOAD (Dockerfile:8). The comment explains why both: an INSTALL that succeeds while LOAD fails would ship green and then answer every question with citations silently disabled.
2. rag._load_fts() (rag.py:203-251) already suppresses repeated failed INSTALL attempts, which reach out to extensions.duckdb.org.

New for Lambda: HOME is not writable, so the DuckDB extension directory must be pre-set or pointed at /tmp.
design:
Base on the AWS Lambda Python base image or a slim Python image with the Lambda Runtime Interface Client. Add the Lambda Web Adapter (layer or COPY --from), set AWS_LWA_INVOKE_MODE=response_stream and AWS_LWA_PORT to match uvicorn.

Bake in: the prebuilt .duckdb artifact, the 2.4MB rag_documents.duckdb corpus, the FTS extension, static/ (63KB index.html + 206KB vendored chart.umd.min.js - already vendored, no CDN dependency).

Drop from the image: the 531MB of CSVs. They are build inputs only and move to S3, read by the offline refresh job, never by the serving function.
acceptance_criteria: Image builds and is under 1GB. Cold start under 5s measured on real Lambda. Citations work (FTS loads without network). Static assets serve.

title: Move the response cache to DynamoDB
description:
The response cache is load-bearing for cost and for degraded-mode service, not just latency.

Today it is a module dict persisted to a local JSON file (app.py:822, _load_cache/_save_cache at app.py:875-916, _cache_put at app.py:1424-1431). Under Lambda each container gets its own copy, so the hit rate collapses toward zero and nearly every request costs an LLM call.

It also matters when quota is exhausted: DAILY_CAP_MSG and QUOTA_MSG both tell the user the cached example answers still work (app.py:110, app.py:121). With a per-container cache that promise breaks.

warm_cache.py becomes MORE important on Lambda, since it is what populates the shared cache so the first real request already hits.
design:
DynamoDB table, PK = the existing cache key (CACHE_VERSION prefix + normalized question, app.py:841). Store the SSE frame list as the item body.

Preserve all four existing semantics, each of which exists for a reason documented in the code:
1. CACHE_VERSION prefixing so a prompt change orphans stale answers (app.py:632-648).
2. LRU touch-on-hit, NOT FIFO - warm starter answers are the highest-value entries and are never re-inserted, so FIFO would evict exactly them (see the comment at app.py:823-833).
3. MAX_CACHE_ENTRIES cap, enforced on load as well as insert.
4. The dead-citation-link pruning in _load_cache() that drops entries containing LegislationDetail.aspx.

Items are small (the persisted file is ~14KB for the current set), so on-demand billing is pennies. Consider a TTL attribute to let old versions self-expire.
acceptance_criteria: Cache hits are served across cold starts and across concurrent instances. warm_cache.py populates the shared cache and a subsequent request from a fresh container hits it. Prompt-version invalidation and LRU eviction both verified by test.

title: Externalize the per-IP rate limiter (DynamoDB or WAF) and rework client-IP for CloudFront
description:
GATES CUTOVER. Do not deploy to Lambda without this.

ip_requests is a module-level dict of IP -> list of timestamps (app.py:151-198), with a 5/min cap. Under Lambda every concurrent container holds an independent dict, so the cap is effectively unenforced.

This is an AVAILABILITY risk, not a billing one. Both providers are hard-capped by construction: OpenRouter free tier stops at 50 req/day, and the Cerebras key is prepaid with no auto-recharge - it stops at zero with HTTP 402 and the user sees QUOTA_MSG (app.py:121). Neither can generate a surprise charge. What an unthrottled client CAN do is drain the prepaid balance in an afternoon and leave the bot serving out-of-credit until topped up, and burn Lambda GB-seconds at ~460 GB-s per pathological request (3 retries at 16s base delay plus two 90s stream timeouts, all time.sleep and all billed).

Second half of this task: _client_ip() (app.py:151-180) trusts forwarded headers only when the immediate peer is in TRUSTED_PROXY_IPS, which is set to the Docker bridge gateway today. Lambda has no stable peer address, so this must be reworked for the CloudFront header chain.
design:
Two options for the limiter, pick during implementation: (a) DynamoDB with TTL - table keyed on client IP, conditional-write counter, TTL for free expiry, no VPC needed; or (b) a CloudFront/WAF rate-based rule, which never invokes Lambda at all and is therefore strictly better for cost, at the price of less control over the response body.

Recommend WAF as the primary defence plus reserved concurrency as the hard compute ceiling, with the DynamoDB limiter only if per-user messaging matters.

For client IP: use CloudFront-Viewer-Address or the CloudFront-appended X-Forwarded-For rather than an IP allowlist. Preserve the existing anti-spoofing property - a client reaching the origin directly must not be able to forge the header.
acceptance_criteria: Rate limit holds across concurrent Lambda instances, demonstrated with a burst test. Reserved concurrency set. A direct-to-origin request cannot spoof its client IP.

title: [epic] Migrate Lou to AWS Lambda serverless (scale-to-zero)
description:
Migrate the self-hosted louisville-bot container to AWS Lambda behind CloudFront, scale-to-zero, ~0 dollars idle. Full analysis and evidence: LOU_MIGRATION_COMPAT.md (2026-08-28).

Verdict: Lambda-compatible with refactor. No architectural blocker. None of the three Cloud Run disqualifiers survives: no websockets or gateway sockets, no connection pool (DuckDB is embedded, in-process), worst-case request 230s vs the 900s cap. Cloud Run would be ~8h vs ~34h for identical cost; Lambda was chosen deliberately for portfolio value (DynamoDB state externalization, response streaming, IaC).

Target: Lambda container image + Lambda Web Adapter response streaming, Function URL behind CloudFront, S3, DynamoDB for shared mutable state, no VPC, no NAT, no API Gateway REST.

Key measured finding: the app rebuilds its analytical DB from 531MB of CSVs on every boot (8.7s, 1.94GB RSS). A prebuilt DuckDB file measures 113MB, 2.4s cold init, 415MB RSS, 0.03s aggregates over 2.26M rows. That single change removes the largest Lambda liability and is worth doing on the current self-hosted box regardless (see louisville-open-data-41y, the 4-min cold start).

Phases: 0 de-risk (spike + artifact) -> 1 instance-independent state -> 2 package and IaC -> 3 cutover.
design:
Sequence: Phase 0 must complete first. The LWA-through-CloudFront streaming spike is the single assumption the whole target rests on; if SSE does not survive CloudFront the verdict flips to Cloud Run, so it runs before any build work. The prebuilt-DuckDB artifact is target-independent and pays off immediately on the current deployment.

Phase 1 items (rate limiter, response cache, stats) are the actual cost of Lambda over Cloud Run: all three are process-local module state that Cloud Run preserves and Lambda does not. They are independent of each other and can run in parallel.

Estimated ~34h total. Projected steady-state cost ~0.15 dollars/month, 0 dollars idle, ~23 percent of the Lambda always-free tier.
notes:
Execution order (all IDs are children of this epic):

PHASE 0 — De-risk. Nothing else starts until these land.
  * n0b  AWS account + billing alarm + IaC bootstrap  (HUMAN)
  * 4l4  SSE-through-LWA-through-CloudFront spike  [dep: n0b]  <- GATES THE TARGET
  * e5n  prebuilt DuckDB artifact (8.7s/1.94GB -> 2.4s/415MB measured)

PHASE 1 — Make the app instance-independent. Parallelizable; this is the real cost of Lambda over Cloud Run.
  * 69m  externalize the per-IP rate limiter + CloudFront client-IP  <- GATES CUTOVER
  * bb0  response cache -> DynamoDB
  * far  stats off local disk, /api/health shape preserved
  * cgx  logging to stdout
  * 5pg  trim billed-idle (time.sleep(3), retry ladder, stream timeouts)

PHASE 2 — Package and infrastructure.
  * n8w  Lambda container image  [dep: 4l4, e5n]
  * i0q  IaC: Lambda + Function URL + CloudFront + S3 + DynamoDB  [dep: n8w, n0b]
  * 0nu  data refresh -> EventBridge Scheduler  [dep: e5n, bb0]
  * 8pf  rotate secrets into SSM  (HUMAN)

PHASE 3 — Cutover.
  * 5cn  re-point monitoring + CloudWatch alarms  [dep: i0q, far]
  * lla  cutover: parallel deploy, warm cache, verify, DNS  [dep: everything]

Two human handoffs are on the critical path (n0b gates the spike, 8pf gates cutover) — start them first.

e5n also resolves louisville-open-data-41y (cold start exceeds 4 min under host load) and is worth shipping to the current self-hosted container even if the migration stalls. 5cn carries forward louisville-open-data-8uk (Cerebras prepaid-balance alert).

title: Rotate the OpenRouter API key before prod rollout
description:

title: Add OpenRouter as primary inference provider (Cerebras paid as fallback)
description:
A free OpenRouter model becomes the primary; the Cerebras pay-as-you-go key stays as the fallback.

Blocker in the current design: provider config is GLOBAL, not per-client. make_client() and make_paid_client() both read the same LLM_BASE_URL, and _call_with_model_fallback passes the SAME model id to the fallback client. That works when both keys are Cerebras; it breaks across providers, where the primary needs openrouter.ai/api/v1 + an OpenRouter slug (e.g. 'x/y:free') and the fallback needs api.cerebras.ai/v1 + gpt-oss-120b.

Work: per-client base_url + model (env: OPENROUTER_API_KEY / OPENROUTER_BASE_URL / OPENROUTER_MODEL, keeping CEREBRAS_PAID_API_KEY + MODEL for the fallback), plumbed through generate_sql / interpret_results_stream / refine_interpretation_stream and the 404 model-fallback resolver. Tier labels ('free'/'paid') should name the provider so dev mode and logs stay honest.

Rate-limit note: OpenRouter caps :free models at 20 RPM and 50 requests/day (1,000/day once $10 of credits has been purchased). The bot makes 2-3 LLM calls per question, so 50/day is ~16-25 questions/day before the fallback carries everything.
acceptance_criteria: Primary (OpenRouter) and fallback (Cerebras) each use their own base URL and model id; a primary failure falls back cross-provider; existing quota/429/404 handling still passes; verified live against both providers.
close_reason: Shipped 2026-08-18: OpenRouter primary (nemotron-3-super-120b-a12b:free) with Cerebras gpt-oss-120b fallback, deployed to prod via --env-file. Verified by startup log + live question through louisville.raylytics.io.

title: Handle Cerebras 402 payment_required: honest user error + paid-tier fallback
description:
Cerebras retired the always-free tier (~2026-07-21) in favor of a $5 Free Trial that expires after 30 days. The free CEREBRAS_API_KEY now returns HTTP 402 payment_required on every call. Two defects surface from this:

1. app.py classifies the 402 as an unknown error and tells the user 'I couldn't turn that into a query. Try rewording it' — completely wrong and unfixable by the user. The project is fine telling users the model API needs more funding from the developer.
2. analytics_agent._call_with_retry only falls back to the paid client on openai.RateLimitError (429). A 402 never triggers the paid fallback, so a configured, working CEREBRAS_PAID_API_KEY sits unused and every live query fails.

Verified 2026-08-18: free key -> 402 payment_required, paid key -> 200 on gpt-oss-120b.
acceptance_criteria: A 402/quota error surfaces a funding-specific message (not 'reword your question'); a quota failure on the free client falls back to the paid client when one is configured; tests cover both.
close_reason: Fixed in aaf4182: is_quota_error + QUOTA_MSG, paid fallback on 402 with a 15-min latch, and single-key (paid) operation. Verified live against Cerebras.

title: Run the louisville-bot container as a non-root user (needs volume chown)
description:
RUNBOOK — run the container as a non-root user (needs a coordinated volume chown)

Why human: adding USER to the Dockerfile is one line, but the existing named
volumes louisville-state (/state) and louisville-logs (/logs) are root-owned and
WRITABLE by the app (stats.json, response cache, rotating logs). A non-root
process can't write them, so flipping USER without chowning the live volumes
would silently break stats + logging in prod. This must be sequenced with a
server-side chown during a deploy — not a repo-only change.

Steps:
1. Pick a uid/gid (e.g. 10001). Add to Dockerfile before CMD:
   RUN adduser --system --uid 10001 appuser
   USER appuser
2. On the server, during the deploy (container stopped): chown the volumes to
   that uid, e.g.
   docker run --rm -v louisville-state:/state -v louisville-logs:/logs alpine \
     chown -R 10001:10001 /state /logs
   (louisville-data stays root-owned; it is mounted read-only.)
3. Recreate the container from the new image (same run command). Verify:
   - /api/health returns ok, /api/usage increments (stats writable),
   - logs still appear in the louisville-logs volume.
4. Roll back by reverting the Dockerfile + restarting the prev image if writes fail.

description:

title: The /api/ask flow is untested end-to-end; suite is not CI/clean-clone runnable
description:
event_stream (the product) has no end-to-end test. No test POSTs to /api/ask via TestClient; the only endpoint test is /api/config. Rate limiting, cache write/replay, SSE event ordering, dev/non-dev split, and the free->paid retry path as wired in event_stream are unexercised. Some "tests" slice app.py SOURCE TEXT (tests/test_rag.py:450 does src[src.index("def event_stream():"):] and asserts on strings) -- that is lint, not behavior.

Also: the module fixture is load_all_data("data") but data/ is gitignored, and .github/workflows/ has only uptime.yml -- no test workflow. The suite is effectively local-to-one-machine and cannot run in CI or from a clean clone.

Component: tests/ + CI.

Suggested direction: add TestClient-based SSE tests with a small fixture dataset + stubbed LLM client; add a GitHub Actions test workflow; commit a tiny sample data slice or a synthetic loader for tests.
design: TestClient SSE tests over event_stream with a fake LLM + tiny fixture data; add a CI workflow that can run without the gitignored prod data.
notes: Phase-0 harness landed: tests/test_ask_endpoint.py drives POST /api/ask through the real router + real DuckDB with a fake LLM (9 tests) — covers SSE event ordering, dev/non-dev humanization split, off-topic guard, empty-result path, blank/malformed input, per-IP rate-limit cap, and cache write/replay + dev-mode-no-cache. REMAINING on this issue: CI workflow (.github) + a synthetic clean-clone fixture so the suite runs without the gitignored data/ dir.
close_reason: Fixed both halves: phase-0 gave /api/ask an end-to-end behavioral suite (test_ask_endpoint.py); phase-2 makes the suite CI/clean-clone runnable — conftest require_data gate skips data-bound tests when the gitignored CSVs are absent (clean-clone sim: 380 passed/57 skipped/0 errors), plus a GitHub Actions tests.yml. Full local run 437 passed.

title: A chart-render exception aborts the SSE read loop and loses the answer text
description:
static/index.html builds the chart with new Chart(...) inside the SSE read loop try-block (~:1352); Chart.js is loaded only from cdn.jsdelivr.net (:8) with no SRI/CSP. If jsdelivr is blocked (adblock/privacy extensions frequently block it, captive networks, offline), the chart event throws ReferenceError, the outer catch fires, and ALL remaining SSE events are skipped -- so the interpretation (sent AFTER the chart) never renders and the user sees "Something went wrong: Chart is not defined" instead of a chartless answer.

Component: static/index.html SSE handler + CDN dependency.

Suggested direction: guard with typeof Chart !== undefined (or per-event try/catch) so a chart failure degrades to a chartless answer; consider self-hosting Chart.js and adding SRI + a CSP.
design: Isolate chart rendering in its own try/catch; never let a viz failure drop the answer. Self-host + SRI Chart.js.
close_reason: Fixed: chart rendering wrapped in its own try/catch with a typeof-Chart guard, so a chart failure degrades to a chartless answer instead of aborting the SSE loop and losing the interpretation. JS syntax + brace balance verified; source-assertion regression test added. (Self-hosting Chart.js + SRI/CSP remains tracked under e8d.)

title: pull_arcgis pagination skips records when server caps page size below --batch-size
description:
pull_arcgis.py:108-127 advances offsets by the REQUESTED batch_size (offset = page * batch_size), not by records actually returned. If maxRecordCount=1000 and the user passes --batch-size 5000: page 0 returns rows 0-999 with exceededTransferLimit=true (no break), page 1 requests offset 5000 -> rows 1000-4999 are never fetched. The CSV is written anyway with ~20% of the data and no error.

Safe only because the default 1000 happens to be <= typical hosted-layer caps. pull_socrata streams atomically; pull_arcgis both mis-pages and writes non-atomically (to_csv direct, no .part swap).

Component: pull_arcgis.py.

Suggested direction: offset += len(features); assert page length; adopt the .part + os.replace pattern pull_socrata already uses.
design: Advance offset by returned count, not requested size; write via .part + os.replace like pull_socrata.
close_reason: Fixed: offset advances by actual returned count with exceededTransferLimit-driven termination (no more skipped records when the server caps page size below --batch-size); a short final tally now warns instead of silently writing a partial file. save_data is now atomic (.part + os.replace). 5 regression tests added (capped server, exact multiple, empty, atomic CSV+JSON).

title: summary_agency_contractors join fan-out inflates contractor spend (~$6.8M phantom)
description:
active_contractors has duplicate FULLNAME rows (3231 rows / 3112 distinct; multiple license categories per business). summary_agency_contractors (city.yaml:223-235) joins expenditures on LOWER(payee)=LOWER(FULLNAME) and SUM(e.extended_amount), so each expenditure row is counted once per duplicate license row.

Measured on real data FY2022-24: join-as-written = $23,763,749 vs deduped = $16,960,382 -> $6.8M phantom spend in total_contractor_spend, served via an advertised summary table. contractor_count (COUNT DISTINCT) is fine; the dollar column is wrong.

Component: cities/louisville/city.yaml summary SQL.

Suggested direction: dedupe active_contractors to one row per FULLNAME before the join (or join on a distinct-name subquery).
design: Join expenditures against SELECT DISTINCT FULLNAME, not the raw multi-license table.
close_reason: Fixed: join now dedupes contractor names; summary total matches deduped recompute exactly, ~$37M phantom removed. Regression test added. Re-warm the licensed-contractors starter answer after deploy (cached number changes).

title: SQL prompt advertises six old-era columns the loader silently drops
description:
The expenditures table schema is built from the 2018+ CSVs; the old-era (2008-2017) insert path aligns with df = df[existing_cols] (data_model.py:127-136), silently discarding any mapped column not present in the 2018+ files. Verified against loaded data: sub_agency, department, sub_department, stimulus_type, payment_amount, payment_void_date are ALL absent from the loaded expenditures table.

Yet the SQL-generation prompt (app.py:499) tells the model "2008-2017: has sub_agency, department, sub_department, stimulus_type, payment_amount, payment_void_date", city.yaml:120-127 maps them, and the data dictionary documents them. Any generated query using them (e.g. "which 2015 payments were voided?", "break down by sub-agency") hits a DuckDB binder error; 2008-2017 check-level amounts and void dates are unrecoverably absent.

Component: data_model loader + app.py sql_system prompt + city.yaml.

Suggested direction: either preserve the old-era columns at load (union schema) or remove them from the prompt/dictionary so the model never emits them. Prompt and schema must agree.
design: Union the era schemas at load, OR strip the phantom columns from prompt+dictionary. The two must not disagree.
close_reason: Fixed: SQL prompt (app.py) and data dictionary (city.yaml) now match the loaded unified schema — the six dropped old-era columns are marked NOT queryable, so the model won't emit binder-error SQL. Contract regression test added (test_sql_prompt_never_advertises_columns_the_loader_dropped). Preserving the old-era columns via a schema union remains a possible future enhancement but is not required to close the contradiction.

title: Monitoring healthcheck ping UUID and ntfy topic are committed to a PUBLIC repo
description:
RUNBOOK — rotate + de-git monitoring secrets (needs external account access)

Why human: rotating live third-party credentials (healthchecks.io check UUID, ntfy topic) and scrubbing git history require account access and an irreversible history rewrite on a PUBLIC repo — not for an unattended agent.

Steps:
1. healthchecks.io: create a NEW check (or regenerate the ping URL) for 'louisville-bot'; note the new UUID.
2. ntfy: pick a new unguessable topic (or move to an authenticated ntfy instance).
3. Move both OUT of monitoring/louisville-bot-heartbeat.sh into env vars / a gitignored config the LaunchAgent sources (CHECK_UUID, NTFY_TOPIC); update the script to read them from the environment.
4. Update the LaunchAgent (com.raylytics.louisville-bot-healthcheck) and the bd memory 'louisville-uptime-alerting' with the new identifiers.
5. Scrub the old UUID + topic from history (git filter-repo) and force-push, OR (lower risk) just DELETE the old healthchecks check + abandon the topic so a kept-green ping can't hide an outage.
6. Verify with the drill in monitoring/README.md: stop the container, confirm the alert fires to the new topic within ~4 min.

Evidence: repo is PUBLIC (gh repo view). The UUID + topic are in monitoring/louisville-bot-heartbeat.sh and referenced from CLAUDE.md.

## Prior description (preserved on handoff)

monitoring/louisville-bot-heartbeat.sh hardcodes CHECK_UUID (healthchecks.io) and NTFY_TOPIC (air-server-evan-...). The repo is public (gh repo view: visibility PUBLIC). Anyone can curl hc-ping.com/<UUID> every minute to keep the dead-mans-switch green during a real outage (the whole design is that WITHHOLDING the ping is the alert), and anyone can publish spoofed pushes to / subscribe on the open ntfy topic.

Failure: the alerting layer built after the 2026-08-11 five-hour outage is fully defeatable/spoofable by any reader of the repo.

Component: monitoring/ + repo secrecy.

Suggested direction: rotate the healthchecks check and ntfy topic, move both into env/secrets (gitignored), and scrub them from git history.
design: Rotate + move to gitignored env; scrub history. Treat ping URL and ntfy topic as secrets.

title: Unauthenticated DELETE /api/cache lets anyone wipe the response cache
description:
DELETE /api/cache (app.py:678-693) has no auth, no rate limit (the limiter only guards /api/ask), and no origin/CSRF check. curl -X DELETE https://louisville.raylytics.io/api/cache from anywhere clears all cached answers and persists the wipe.

Failure: an attacker deletes the cache on a loop; every question (including warm-cache starter answers that once masked the qwen deprecation) then hits the free-tier LLM, burning quota and degrading cold-start UX. Compounds with the site-wide rate-limit bug.

Component: app.py cache admin endpoints.

Suggested direction: require a shared-secret/admin token for cache mutation (and ideally for GET too), or bind these endpoints to localhost only.
design: Gate all /api/cache mutations behind an admin token or localhost-only binding.
close_reason: Fixed: DELETE /api/cache now requires X-Admin-Token, fail-closed without ADMIN_TOKEN. refresh_data.py sends the token. Tests cover disabled/401/200. DEPLOY: set -e ADMIN_TOKEN=... on the container.

title: Per-IP rate limit collapses to a site-wide 5 req/min behind the Cloudflare tunnel
description:
check_ip_rate_limit buckets on request.client.host (app.py:880). In production the path is Cloudflare -> cloudflared on the host -> localhost:8000 -> container (per CLAUDE.md), so every real user request arrives from the same peer IP (the Docker bridge gateway). Uvicorn is not started with --proxy-headers and the app never reads X-Forwarded-For / CF-Connecting-IP, so all traffic shares ONE bucket.

Failure: two users asking 3 questions each in a minute lock each other out; a single curl loop rate-limits the whole site. Live-observed side evidence: /api/usage shows rpm_remaining:0 after a handful of test requests from one client.

Component: app.py rate limiting + Dockerfile/uvicorn launch.

Suggested direction: run uvicorn with --proxy-headers (and trusted proxy config), then key the limiter on CF-Connecting-IP / the real client IP; add a test.
design: Key the limiter on the forwarded client IP; do not trust it without --proxy-headers + a trusted-hosts allowlist.
close_reason: Fixed in code: _client_ip prefers CF-Connecting-IP so the per-IP limit keys on the real client, not the shared tunnel peer; Dockerfile adds --proxy-headers. Test proves distinct client IPs get separate buckets. DEPLOY: rebuild image (Dockerfile CMD changed).

title: Technology/cybersecurity starter question returns 0 rows — model guesses category keywords absent from the data
description: 'What does Louisville Metro spend on technology and cybersecurity?' generates spend_category ILIKE '%technology%' OR '%cybersecurity%' — zero rows in the entire dataset — so the bot answers that the city spends nothing on technology, and adds a false claim that FY2025 is still in progress (2026 is the partial year). Reality: agency_canonical='Metro Technology Services' totals $242.3M, and the real categories are Computer Software / Computer Hardware / Cloud Computing Services / Computer Equipment. Fix: add a topic-vocabulary section to the SQL prompt mapping common topical words to actual data values (tech -> the Metro Technology Services agency + Computer%/Software%/Cloud% categories), plus a general rule to prefer agency_canonical for departmental topics and never invent category keywords. The 0-row answer is correctly not cached, so the starter question hits the LLM live every time.
close_reason: Fixed through four rounds of prod verification. Started as: spend_category ILIKE '%technology%' matched ZERO rows citywide, so the bot said Louisville spends nothing on technology (plus a false 'FY2025 still in progress' claim). Fixes: (1) topic-vocabulary prompt section mapping everyday words to real data values, with the rule that an empty topical filter means the filter is wrong, not that spending is absent; (2) data_facts now names 2026 as in-progress and 2025 as the most recent COMPLETE year — false-partial claim gone; (3) prose alone didn't stop the model ANDing department AND category ($3.7-4.3M vs real $22.4M/$19.9M), so a copy-exact UNION query is prescribed (same remedy as the grant total); (4) with both figures right the model summed them into a $42.3M 'combined' total — double-counting the overlap — so the tech bullet forbids combining the two views and the refine rubric gained a general rule: only add mutually exclusive slices. Final prod answer states $22.4M and $19.9M separately with an honest caveat, no invented total.

title: Schema description is non-deterministic — CACHE_VERSION changes every restart, pruning the whole cache on every deploy
description: get_compact_schema_description runs SELECT DISTINCT ... LIMIT 12 with no ORDER BY, so DuckDB returns enum values in arbitrary parallel-scan order. Verified: two processes over identical data produce different schema hashes (2ff353c85291 vs 6c85dad3fea6). Consequences: (1) CACHE_VERSION (hash of assembled prompts incl. schema) differs on every startup, so the startup pruner deletes ALL cached answers on every deploy/restart — observed pruning 9 entries on a deploy that changed no prompt text; starter questions then hit the LLM live, slow and exposed to the hallucination risk the cache exists to avoid; (2) the SQL system prompt itself churns between restarts, defeating provider prompt caching and making behavior non-reproducible. Fix: ORDER BY the DISTINCT enum queries in both schema description builders + a determinism test.
close_reason: Fixed: added ORDER BY 1 to the DISTINCT enum/sample queries in both schema-description builders. Verified deterministic across three separate processes (identical hashes; previously differed run to run). Regression tests assert enum values are sorted and repeated calls are identical — both fail with the ORDER BY reverted. This restores the response cache (it was being pruned on every restart, sending starter questions to the LLM live) and stabilizes the SQL prompt across restarts.

title: 'Salary plus benefits' hallucination survives (quoted anti-phrase imitated); follow-up 'is that true?' wrongly rejected as off-topic
description: Two failures on the highest-paid starter question: (1) the refined answer appended 'total compensation (salary plus benefits)' — the literal phrase both prompts quote as forbidden; second instance of negative-example imitation (same mechanism as the quoted-SQL bug in 6ni). (2) The follow-up 'Is [that claim] true?' hit the off-topic guard because the SQL prompt gives no route for verification/meta questions about the prior answer — it should decompose the claim via SQL (select the pay component columns). close_reason: Fixed and verified through prod (8c5fcca). (1) Benefits hallucination: second confirmed instance of negative-example imitation — both prompts quoted 'plus benefits' as the forbidden phrase and the model reproduced it. All quoted anti-phrases replaced with positive factual rules (data contains pay components only, no benefits info) and summary_top_salaries dictionary now states benefits are NOT included. title: Grant answer total is model arithmetic over 102 rows — wrong by $54M ($1.12B vs true $1.17B)
description: The cached 'how much grant funding' answer states $1.12B total and ~$150M remainder; true values are $1,174.2M and $162.4M (top-10 list is exactly correct). Results carry 102 fund rows with no total row, so the LLM summed them mentally — and the refiner can't verify 102-row sums either. Fix: (a) prompt bullet tells the model to compute the grand total in SQL (GROUP BY ROLLUP pattern) for 'how much overall' questions; (b) refine rubric forbids totaling long lists — if no total row exists, don't state an overall figure; (c) re-warm the grant answer and verify the total matches SQL.

Fixes: grant bullet is now a copy-exactly ROLLUP query against summary_grant_funding (locally verified, TOTAL row first); the anti-example prose no longer quotes SQL; refine rubric forbids totaling long lists (no total row = no overall figure). Regenerated through prod: SQL matches verbatim, 103 rows, answer states $1.174 billion exactly, remainder described qualitatively. Cached. title: Highest-paid-positions answer is wrong: interpreter unit/scope hallucination + summary_top_salaries design flaws
description: Baked-in starter question produces a badly wrong answer. Layer 1 (interpretation, worst): gpt-oss-120b converted $192,770.57 to '$192.77M' (thousands->millions, every row), claimed the data 'spans FY2008-FY2026' (salary_data is CalYear 2021-2026 only — the model leaked the EXPENDITURES table's scope from the schema prompt), and invented 'salary plus benefits' (YTD_Total has no benefits). NOTE: EMS EMT-Paramedic II ~$140K avg is REAL (OT-heavy: ~$100K rate + ~$50K OT, max $222K in 2025) — data is right, presentation lacks the OT nuance.
close_reason: Fixed all layers and verified in prod (f5024fb deployed). title: Decide the LLM provider stance after OpenRouter's free-tier degradation (2026-08-31)
description:
## Why this needs you

This is a money/policy call. On 2026-08-31 OpenRouter's free nemotron slug
(the pinned primary) degraded hard: HTTP-200 responses with no choices,
in-stream "Upstream error from Nvidia: Service temporarily overloaded", and
streams that stayed open while dribbling a few tokens a minute. A user hit it
live ("LLM response contained no choices"). The vetted backup free slug
(poolside/laguna-s-2.1:free) answered correctly but at 39-61s/question
(eval/results/20260831-125815-laguna-check.md).

The code now defends itself — deployed the same day: generic provider errors
and dead/stalled streams fail over to the Cerebras paid key (STREAM_STALL_SECONDS=20,
LLM_TIMEOUT_SECONDS=30 on the container). But while OpenRouter limps rather
than fails, first-token latency on live questions is still 12-35s, against
~2s when Cerebras serves (23/23 on the eval at ~$0.001-0.002/question).

## The decision

Pick one (all are container-env-only changes, no rebuild — see CLAUDE.md):

1. KEEP free-first (status quo). $0/day; slow-but-answered when OpenRouter
   struggles; the stall guard caps the pain at ~20s per LLM call before
   Cerebras takes over.
2. Cerebras-first: remove OPENROUTER_API_KEY from the container env.
   Fast (~2s/question) and consistent; costs roughly $0.05-0.15/day at
   current traffic; balance was $9.62 on 2026-08-18 — check it, and note the
   out-of-credit case now pages via the healthcheck (8uk).
3. Buy $10 of OpenRouter credits: raises the free-model daily cap 50 -> 1000
   requests/day and may improve routing, but does nothing for an overloaded
   upstream like today's.

## How to apply

- Option 2: recreate the container without OPENROUTER_API_KEY (runbook step 3c
  grep list minus that var). Re-run `python eval/run_eval.py --provider env`
  after; re-warm the starter cache.
- Option 1: nothing to do; optionally revisit OPENROUTER_MODEL when
  https://openrouter.ai/nvidia/nemotron-3-super-120b-a12b/status recovers.
close_reason: Decision by Evan 2026-08-31: keep free-first (option 1). OpenRouter's free nemotron stays primary with the Cerebras paid key as fallback; the same-day guards (provider-error/404 failover, whole-draft retry, STREAM_STALL_SECONDS=20, LLM_TIMEOUT_SECONDS=30) cap the pain at ~20-30s per LLM call before Cerebras takes over. Nothing to apply on the container. If nemotron's upstream degradation persists, revisiting OPENROUTER_MODEL (re-benchmark per CLAUDE.md) is the lever — not a policy change.

title: DuckDB 1.5.1 returns swapped column VALUES for a window partitioned by a column that is also filtered with <> in the same SELECT
description: Reproduced 2026-08-30 on duckdb 1.5.1 (python): SELECT tbl, col, val FROM (SELECT tbl, col, val, weight, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY tbl, col ORDER BY weight DESC) AS rn FROM _value_index WHERE col <> 'x' AND val ILIKE '%mayor%') WHERE rn <= 2 returns rows with the tbl and col values SWAPPED while cursor.description still reports (tbl, col, val). Same with QUALIFY. Putting the filter in its own CTE and the window in a second CTE returns correct rows. Dropping the col <> predicate also fixes it. Risk: LLM-generated SQL of that shape (ROW_NUMBER over agency_canonical with an agency_canonical <> filter) would silently mislabel rows in an answer. grounding._elsewhere uses the CTE shape with a regression test (tests/test_grounding.py::test_elsewhere_returns_table_column_value). TODO: minimize + report upstream, check whether a newer duckdb fixes it, consider pinning.

title: Move the data refresh job to EventBridge Scheduler
description:
The only offline job that must survive the move. It is manual today - no cron exists for it anywhere in the repo.

Chain: refresh_data.py pulls the ArcGIS and Socrata datasets to CSV and rebuilds contractor profiles; rag.py ingest pulls Legistar into rag_documents.duckdb; then the new --materialize step (louisville-open-data-e5n) produces the DuckDB artifact.

Watch the 15-minute Lambda cap. A full pull of 19 years of expenditure datasets plus SOS lookups will likely exceed it - refresh_data.py already has --pull-only, --skip-pull and --skip-sos flags that could split the work, but CodeBuild or Step Functions may be the cleaner answer.

Note refresh_data.py:224 currently DELETEs http://localhost:8000/api/cache to clear the response cache after a refresh. That has to become a call against the new endpoint with ADMIN_TOKEN, or a direct DynamoDB operation once the cache moves (louisville-open-data-bb0).
design:
Preferred shape: EventBridge Scheduler triggers a build (CodeBuild if the 15-min cap binds, Lambda if not) that writes CSVs to S3, produces the .duckdb artifact, rebuilds the container image, and deploys it. That keeps the build plane fully separate from the serving plane.

The graph/ scripts (Neo4j) stay local tooling - neo4j is not in requirements.txt and the serving app never touches it. Do not migrate them.

Post-refresh, warm_cache.py must run against the new URL to repopulate the shared cache.
acceptance_criteria: A scheduled run produces a fresh artifact and a deployed image with no manual step. Cache is cleared and re-warmed automatically. Failure alerts somewhere a human sees.

title: Trim billed-idle time on the request path
description:
On a long-lived container these waits are free. On Lambda every second is billed at the function memory size.

1. time.sleep(3) on the hot path (app.py:1252) - a deliberate anti-RPM pause between the SQL result and the interpretation call. 3s of pure billed idle on every uncached question.

2. The retry ladder: MAX_RETRIES 3 at RETRY_BASE_DELAY 16s (analytics_agent.py:29-30, time.sleep at analytics_agent.py:205) - up to 48s of billed sleep.

3. Two 90s stream timeouts (app.py:1289 interpretation, app.py:1382 refinement).

Worst case is ~230s for a single request, which at 2GB is ~460 GB-s - about 870 such requests would exhaust the monthly free tier. Compounds with the rate-limiter gap (louisville-open-data-69m).
design:
Make all three configurable by env with the current values as defaults, so tuning does not need a code change.

For the 3s pause specifically: it exists to avoid back-to-back RPM hits at the provider. On Lambda the same protection is better served by the retry ladder that already exists, so it can likely be removed outright - but verify against the OpenRouter 20 req/min free-tier cap before deleting.

Do NOT remove the retry ladder itself. It is what makes the provider fallback work, and the daily-cap path already bypasses it correctly (is_daily_cap_error routes straight to fallback rather than sleeping 16s for a cap that only resets at midnight UTC).
acceptance_criteria: Typical uncached request duration drops by at least 3s. Retry and timeout values settable by env. Provider fallback behaviour unchanged - tests/test_quota_fallback.py and tests/test_model_fallback.py still pass.
close_reason: All three knobs env-tunable in e85333b; the 3s+2s pause defaults to 0 since cef446e (typical uncached request 7.2s -> 2.2s in the eval).

title: Logging to stdout only; drop the /logs RotatingFileHandler
description:
app.py:22 defaults LOG_DIR to /logs and app.py:35-44 attaches a RotatingFileHandler (10MB x 5 backups) to a Docker named volume.

Lambda filesystem is read-only except /tmp, so os.makedirs(/logs) fails. It is already wrapped in try/except so the app degrades rather than crashes - but the file handler silently vanishes and the only signal is a log line about it.

On Lambda, stdout goes to CloudWatch automatically, which is the correct destination. The rotating file handler should be conditional on a writable LOG_DIR rather than attempted-and-swallowed.
design:
Make the file handler opt-in: attach it only when LOG_DIR is set AND writable. Keep it working for the current self-hosted deployment and for local dev so this is not a regression there.

Set CloudWatch log retention to 7 days in IaC - the app logs verbosely (log.info per request plus the debug SSE mirror), projected ~150MB/month ingest which is cents but grows silently at default infinite retention.
acceptance_criteria: Runs clean on a read-only filesystem with no /logs. Structured lines reach CloudWatch. The self-hosted container still writes rotating files when LOG_DIR is writable.
close_reason: Shipped in e35cd36 (see commit message): date_sanity at load; funding failures make /api/health degraded with a reason and the heartbeat escalates it; LOG_DIR opt-in / stdout-only; duckdb>=1.5.5 (bug reproduced on 1.5.1, gone on 1.5.5); contractor_profiles rebuilt on canonical payees with SOS backfill and tracked in git.

title: Move stats off local disk, preserving the /api/health contract
description:
Daily usage counters and the error ring buffer are held in a module dict behind a threading.Lock and persisted to a local JSON file (app.py:203-263). On Lambda they are lost on every container recycle and race across instances.

The constraint that makes this non-trivial: .github/workflows/uptime.yml asserts on the exact shape of /api/health - it reads .status, .model_fallback, and .errors.errors_last_hour, and fails the workflow on status != ok or a non-null model_fallback. Changing the health response shape silently breaks the external uptime monitor, which exists because the 2026-08-11 502 outage ran 5 hours unnoticed.

The heartbeat script (monitoring/louisville-bot-heartbeat.sh) also parses this endpoint every 60s.
design:
Two candidates: DynamoDB atomic counters (UpdateItem ADD) for requests/tokens per day plus a short error list, or drop the persistence entirely in favour of CloudWatch EMF metrics and compute errors_last_hour from a metric query.

EMF is cheaper and more idiomatic but makes /api/health depend on a CloudWatch query, adding latency to an endpoint hit every 60s. DynamoDB keeps the endpoint self-contained. Lean DynamoDB for the health path, EMF additionally for dashboards.

Note /api/health also runs COUNT(*) over every table behind db_lock (app.py:681-704) - cheap on the prebuilt file-backed DB (under 50ms measured) but it is 43,200 invocations/month from the heartbeat. Consider serving counts from a value computed once at init.
acceptance_criteria: /api/health returns the identical JSON shape it does today, verified against the assertions in .github/workflows/uptime.yml. Counters survive a container recycle. Health endpoint responds in under 200ms warm.

title: Deploy/config landmines: stale compose 45s start_period, deploy.sh rsyncs .env, unpinned deps, root container, no CSP/SRI, docs contradiction
description:
Config-hygiene items that are individually minor but each a concrete footgun:

1. docker-compose.yml healthcheck still has start_period: 45s -- the exact value that caused the 2026-08-11 restart-loop outage (cold start can exceed 4 min; CLAUDE.md mandates 600s). deploy.sh also rsyncs .env (real secrets) to the server and uses this compose file. CLAUDE.md already flags compose/deploy.sh as stale, but running either reintroduces a known outage mode with secrets in tow -- prefer deleting/fixing over annotating.
2. requirements.txt is floor-pinned only (all deps bare >=); every server rebuild silently adopts whatever fastapi/duckdb/pandas/openai shipped -- a DuckDB/openai major bump can break or subtly change an unrelated one-line deploy with no diff. Add upper bounds or a lockfile.
3. Dockerfile runs as root (no USER).
4. Chart.js loaded from third-party CDN with no integrity/SRI and no CSP anywhere -- a jsdelivr compromise is arbitrary JS on the prod origin.
5. Docs contradiction: CLAUDE.md says cincinnati/ is a paper config (not runnable) but cities/cincinnati/city.yaml:1 says "RUNNABLE". Also data_model.py:88-89 raises ValueError for the KC pack reader:socrata before checking file existence, so selecting the KC pack crashes at import. One of the docs is wrong.

Component: docker-compose.yml, deploy.sh, requirements.txt, Dockerfile, static/index.html, CLAUDE.md/city.yaml.

Suggested direction: delete or fix the stale deploy artifacts, pin deps, add a non-root USER, add CSP+SRI (self-host Chart.js), reconcile the Cincinnati status.
design: Remove the stale deploy path; pin the dependency layer; add container/browser hardening; reconcile the pack-status docs.
